newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea seeks to heal Kwangju massacre scars.
newsitem.headline: South Korea seeks to heal Kwangju massacre scars.

text.p: In a symbolic act of healing for a tragedy that left deep scars, the South Korean government on Saturday sponsored mourning ceremonies for student victims of a 1980 army massacre in the city of Kwangju.

It was the first time South Korean officials had presided over anniversary events to mark the bloodletting on May 18 ordered by former president Chun Doo Hwan and his successor, Roh Tae-woo, both now serving long jail terms.
Wailing and sobbing, about 200 relatives of the victims gathered in a newly-dedicated cemetery to conduct rites for the dead.
Around 200 people died, by official count, when paratroopers stormed into the southwestern city to crush an armed revolt against martial law declared by then-general Chun in 1979.
But residents say several thousand may have been killed by machinegun fire and bayonets and their bodies buried in unmarked graves or burned.

Elderly female relatives dressed in traditional white mourning robes wept in front of a fruit-laden alter at the "May 18 Cemetery" on hills outside Kwangju where bodies of 124 victims have been laid in fresh graves.
Many of the grieving women cried out the names of sons and daughters who perished.
The remains were moved this month from their original resting place adjacent to the new cemetery.
Kwangju mayor Song Eun-jong presided over the ceremony.
The focal point of the new cemetery is a 40 metre-high (131 foot) memorial in the form of stylised hands clasping an egg, a symbol of life.
Two statues flanking the memorial depict students brandishing rifles in heroic style.
Nearby is a oval-shape structure with photographs of the dead fixed to the walls. Graves with simple granite headstones are laid out in neat rows on a lawn.

A total of 137 bodies of massacre victims lay in the old cemetery. Some relatives have refused to move the remains until the new cemetery is designated a "National Cemetery", whose occupants are honoured as heroes.
Kwangju officials put the death toll from the army rampage at 166, with 47 missing.
"They've been neglected for too long and now they are finally being honoured," said Park Kong-soon, president of the Kwangju Bereaved Families Association.
In front of one new headstone a middle-aged man, Lee Nam, paid respects to his best friend, Kim Dong-soo, who was just 22 and a student at the local Chosun University when he was killed by troops.
"I have lived with guilt for not being there with Dong-soo," he said in an emotion-filled voice.
Meanwhile, about 3,000 students at Chosun University continued mourning rites for a colleague who died of a heart attack during an anti-government protest in March.

The coffin of the student was laid on the back of a truck inside the campus on Friday, and it remained there overnight as students fought sporadic battles with thousands of riot police surrounding the college.
Students hurled blazing molotov cocktails at ranks of police, who responded with volleys of teargas.
This year's anniversary of the Kwangju massacre has added poignancy because of the jailing of Chun and Roh at the end of 1995 on charges of mutiny, treason and corruption.
Chun was sentenced to life in prison and Roh to 17 years, and final appeals were dismissed in April.
